newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Thousands march for jobs in central Belgium.
newsitem.headline: Thousands march for jobs in central Belgium.

text.p: Thousands of people demonstrated peacefully but noisily through this central Belgian city on Thursday, urging the government to clean up its act on job creation.
Police said 6,500 people took part and organisers put it at 9,000 but both estimates were well below the expected 15,000.
The marchers paraded under the slogan "Solidarity before Profit" clad in the red, green and blue of their respective unions.

The march, against the backdrop of company closures, tightening budgetary belts and stubbornly high unemployment, was one of a series that have already taken place or are planned in the run up to a European Union summit in Amsterdam on June 16.
Trade unions want to force the leaders of the 15-member EU to agree rules to allow working hours to be cut in order to open the way for the creation of more employment.
They also want governments to cut the tax costs of employment, to introduce tax policies that encourage jobs, establish a coherent social policy and boost economic growth.

But while governments regularly express concern about the EU's 10.8 percent rate of unemployment and sluggish economic growth, their room for manoeuvre is ringfenced by their efforts to slash budget deficits and debt in preparation for joining the bloc's single currency in 1999.
Feelings have been running high in Belgium since January when steelmaker Clabecq was declared bankrupt, putting 1,800 jobs at risk.
Tempers flared again in February when French carmaker Renault suddenly declared it would close its plant at Vilvoorde near Brussels with the loss of 3,100 jobs.
On Thursday official speeches by trade union leaders were barely audible, smothered by a chorus of disapproval from unionists who demanded that workers themselves speak out.
"This is not a success like the trade unionists say it is," said Clabecq workers' leader Roberto D'Orazio. "It would go much better if workers were allowed to take the stand," he said.
